case_name: Batch of petitions arising from show cause notices/order-in-original concerning Worlds Window Impex India Pvt. Ltd. (and connected matters) v. Union of India & GST authorities
citation: Delhi High Court, judgment reserved 21 September 2026, pronounced 29 September 2026
holding_summary: A Division Bench of Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Bharat Parashar heard a batch of writ petitions challenging show cause notices and orders-in-original imposing personal penalties under Section 122(1A) of the CGST Act, 2017 on persons alleged to have retained the benefit of fraudulently availed input tax credit. The Court held that the expression 'any person' in Section 122(1A) is not confined to a registered or otherwise taxable person and can reach someone who is neither registered nor liable to be registered, provided the statutory conditions are met. However, it held the provision applies only prospectively, to acts or transactions on or after 1 January 2021 (when Section 122(1A) came into force), regardless of when the show cause notice was issued.
why_it_matters: Settles a recurring GST dispute over whether unregistered intermediaries and beneficiaries of fraudulent ITC chains can be penalised under Section 122(1A), while capping the department's ability to reach back to pre-2021 transactions — directly relevant to anyone who has received such a notice for conduct predating the provision.

case_name: Piccadily Agro Industries Ltd. & Piccadily Hotels Private Ltd. v. Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission
citation: APTEL Appeal No. 76 of 2024, decided 17 September 2026
holding_summary: The appellants claimed captive generating plant status for banking benefits, but DHBVNL found that Piccadily Hotels Pvt. Ltd. had consumed only 37.24% of the electricity generated by the designated generating unit in FY 2020-21, below the 51% minimum self-consumption threshold under Rule 3(1)(a)(ii) of the Electricity Rules, 2005, and issued a demand of Rs. 68,03,220 to restore wrongly availed banking benefits. APTEL, per Judicial Member Virender Bhat and Technical Member Ajay Talegaonkar, upheld HERC's denial of captive status, holding that both the prescribed shareholding (at least 26% equity ownership) and the actual annual self-consumption (at least 51%) thresholds must be independently satisfied, and a shortfall in either disqualifies the unit as captive for that year.
why_it_matters: Reinforces that captive power status is tested annually on actual consumption data, not just ownership structuring at the time a plant is set up — a compliance trap for industrial groups running shared or multi-unit captive generation arrangements.

case_name: National Highways Authority of India v. M/s Kurukshetra Expressway Private Ltd.
citation: 2026:DHC:5961; connected appeal Kurukshetra Expressway Private Ltd. v. NHAI, FAO(OS)(COMM) 211/2026, order dated 28 September 2026 (upholding order of 28 July 2026)
holding_summary: KEPL had terminated its 2010 concession agreement with NHAI for the four-laning of the Rohtak-Bawal stretch of NH-71, asserting an 'Indirect Political Force Majeure Event' because COVID-19 and a prolonged farmers' agitation stopped toll collection for more than 180 days in a continuous 365-day period. A majority arbitral award dated 16 August 2024 granted KEPL a Rs. 911.13 crore Termination Payment plus interest. On NHAI's Section 34 challenge, the Delhi High Court set aside the Termination Payment claim and connected interest, holding the tribunal had exceeded the concession agreement's contractual cap on termination liability, while leaving the tribunal's awards on KEPL's other claims undisturbed. A division bench has now upheld that order, rejecting KEPL's appeal against the partial setting-aside.
why_it_matters: Shows courts will enforce a concession agreement's own contractual ceiling on termination compensation even against a tribunal's award, a significant data point for how big-ticket PPP termination disputes get valued and for lenders assessing debt-recovery risk on similarly structured road concessions.

case_name: Nayan Shah and Anr. v. Cheers Interactive (India) Pvt. Ltd. and Ors.
citation: Company Appeal (AT) No. 122 of 2026, NCLAT Principal Bench, New Delhi, decided 18 September 2026
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (Principal Bench, New Delhi)
holding_summary: In a closely-held family quasi-partnership company riven by an irretrievable breakdown of trust between two shareholder groups, the NCLT had found that excluding one group from management and from the fruits of the company's profits, without due process, amounted to oppression under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013, and directed both groups to bid for each other's shares under the supervision of an independent observer using the 'Swiss Challenge' method. NCLAT upheld this, holding that Section 242(2)(b) empowers the NCLT to direct a competitive inter se bidding process between warring shareholder groups where both are willing and able to buy out the other, and that a supervised Swiss Challenge auction was a fair and transparent way to fix the exit price.
why_it_matters: Gives promoters and investors in deadlocked family or joint-venture companies a concrete, tribunal-tested exit mechanism — a supervised inter se auction — as an alternative to protracted oppression-and-mismanagement litigation or forced winding up.

case_name: RA Residences Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. v. RA Associates & Ors.
holding_summary: RA Residences Co-operative Housing Society approached MahaRERA alleging that the promoters, RA Associates, had materially altered the sanctioned building plans for the 'RA Residences' project in Dadar East, Mumbai, by utilising additional Floor Space Index (FSI) for the commercial component without obtaining the allottees' prior informed consent, and had failed to execute conveyance of the property. On appeal, the Maharashtra Real Estate Appellate Tribunal, in Appeal No. AT06/00804/2025 decided 16 September 2026, upheld a penalty equivalent to 2% of the project cost against RA Associates and its partners for the unconsented FSI increase, and directed the promoters to execute conveyance of the residential building and hand over common areas and remaining guest parking to the society within 60 days, rejecting the promoters' plea that conveyance could be deferred pending possible future acquisition of additional FSI or TDR.
why_it_matters: Confirms that a promoter cannot indefinitely withhold conveyance by citing the possibility of acquiring additional FSI or TDR in future, and that altering a sanctioned plan's FSI without the allottees' informed consent attracts a cost-linked penalty — a useful precedent for housing societies pursuing stalled conveyance and FSI-misuse claims against developers.

case_name: Indian Motion Picture Producers' Association v. Member-Petitioners (209 IMPPA Members)
citation: NCLAT Principal Bench, New Delhi, decided 2 October 2026, on appeal from an NCLT Mumbai waiver order
court: National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (Principal Bench, New Delhi)
holding_summary: 209 members of the Indian Motion Picture Producers' Association (IMPPA), a company without share capital, petitioned under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging misuse and diversion of funds, non-disclosure of expenditure, irregularities in circulation of notices and minutes, accounting discrepancies, illegal appointment of two senior vice-presidents, and illegal suspension/expulsion of members. Because IMPPA claimed roughly 1,250 voting-eligible members (requiring support of one-fifth, i.e. about 250, under Section 244(1)(b)), it argued the 209 petitioning members fell short of the statutory threshold. The NCLT, Mumbai Bench, nonetheless waived the threshold requirement. On IMPPA's appeal, a bench of Justice Sharad Kumar Sharma and Technical Members Arun Baroka and Indevar Pandey upheld the waiver, holding that NCLT had properly exercised its statutory discretion under the proviso to Section 244(1)(b) to permit members of a company without share capital to pursue an oppression-and-mismanagement petition despite the numerical shortfall.
why_it_matters: Confirms that tribunals retain broad discretion to waive the one-fifth membership threshold under Section 244(1)(b) for companies without share capital — such as trade, professional or industry associations — letting a numerically short group of members still pursue oppression-and-mismanagement claims against the body's management where the underlying allegations warrant scrutiny.
